section_title: Intentional Torts to Person, Land and Goods

nodes.label: Intentional Torts to Person, Land and Goods
nodes.summary: Trespass to the person (battery, assault, false imprisonment), trespass to land, trespass to goods, conversion, detinue, and defences including consent, self-defence and necessity.

nodes.label: Trespass to the Person Overview
nodes.summary: Trespass to the person encompasses battery, assault, and false imprisonment. These are actionable per se (no proof of damage required). Intent or negligence must be proved.

nodes.label: Battery
nodes.summary: Battery is the intentional and direct application of force to another person without lawful justification or consent. The force need not be hostile or hostile intent is no longer essential. Any physical contact may suffice.

nodes.label: Assault
nodes.summary: Assault is an act which causes the claimant reasonably to apprehend the imminent application of unlawful force. Words alone may constitute assault. Conditional threats may suffice. No actual physical contact required.

nodes.label: False Imprisonment
nodes.summary: False imprisonment is the unlawful and total restraint of the claimant's freedom of movement. No actual physical force required; submission to the defendant's authority suffices. The restraint must be complete.

nodes.label: Trespass to Land
nodes.summary: Trespass to land is the unjustified, direct interference with land in the claimant's exclusive possession. Actionable per se. Includes entering land, remaining on land, or placing objects on land without lawful authority.

nodes.label: Trespass: Airspace and Subsurface
nodes.summary: Ownership of land extends to the airspace above and the subsurface below, but only to such height/depth as is necessary for ordinary use and enjoyment. Aircraft overflight at a reasonable height is not trespass.

nodes.label: Trespass to Goods Overview
nodes.summary: Trespass to goods is the intentional or negligent, direct interference with goods in the claimant's possession. Actionable per se. Includes damaging, moving, or handling goods without authority.

nodes.label: Conversion
nodes.summary: Conversion is an intentional dealing with goods that is seriously inconsistent with the owner's right to possession. Includes taking, using, selling, destroying or refusing to return goods. Remedies include damages and specific delivery.

nodes.label: Detinue
nodes.summary: Detinue is the wrongful detention of goods after a demand for their return. The claimant must have a right to possession and the defendant must have refused to return them. HK position on detinue surviving abolition needs verification.

nodes.label: Defences to Intentional Torts
nodes.summary: Common defences include: consent (express or implied), self-defence (reasonable force), defence of others, defence of property, necessity, lawful authority (police powers, court orders), and discipline (reasonable chastisement).

nodes.label: Medical Consent and Battery
nodes.summary: Medical treatment without consent may constitute battery. The scope of consent and the doctrine of informed consent apply. Emergency treatment without consent may be justified by necessity.

nodes.label: Wong Cheuk Fai v Secretary for Justice [2016] HKCFI 567
nodes.summary: Seed case for battery / trespass to person in HK. Needs paragraph verification.

nodes.label: Leung Ka Fai v Commissioner of Police [2013] HKCFI 890
nodes.summary: Seed case for false imprisonment / unlawful detention in HK. Needs paragraph verification.

nodes.label: Wilson v Pringle [1987] QB 237
nodes.summary: Battery requires hostile intent and direct physical contact. Hostility need not be angry or aggressive.

nodes.label: Verify HK Intentional Tort Leading Cases
nodes.summary: Research and verify HK CFA/CA decisions on trespass to person, conversion, detinue, and defences such as police powers and medical consent.
